caption:
The rule wealthy people use to think about money 👇 and it’s simple enough to teach your kid tonight.

It’s called the Rule of 72. You take 72 and divide it by the interest rate, and you get roughly how many years it takes for money to double.

The good: say your child’s money earns about 7% a year. 72 divided by 7 is about 10. So their money doubles roughly every 10 years, without them adding a cent. Start at 10, and it can double several times before they’re an adult.

The bad, and this is the part nobody teaches: it works in reverse too. Take a credit card charging 22%. 72 divided by 22 is about 3. So a debt they ignore can double in roughly 3 years. Same rule, opposite direction.

That’s the lesson worth giving them. The same force that grows money quietly grows debt just as fast.

Wondering what happens to your kid’s RESP if they don’t go to school? 👇

Good news first: you don’t lose your own money. Your contributions come back to you, tax-free. And an RESP can stay open for 35 years, so a gap year or a late start is no problem at all.

The part to plan for is the rest. The government grants get repaid, and the growth can be taxed unless you move it into your RRSP. There’s a right way to handle each piece, and getting it wrong is where families lose money they didn’t have to.

It’s not the disaster most parents fear, but it is worth knowing before you need to.

caption:
Before your kid taps “pay in 4,” they need to hear this from you.
Buy now, pay later (Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm, Sezzle…) is built to feel harmless. For a teen or young adult, here’s why it isn’t 👇

- It’s not one purchase — it’s a loan. Your teen can have several “pay in 4” plans running across different apps at once, and those small payments quietly add up to more than they can actually afford.

- It’s only “free” if every payment is on time. Miss one due date and late fees stack up — that “free” $50 split can end up costing $65 or more.

- Payments auto-withdraw whether the money’s there or not. If their account comes up short on the scheduled date, the bank adds its own overdraft and NSF fees on top.

- It can hurt their credit before they even have a credit card. Many of these apps now report to the credit bureaus, so one missed payment can dent the score they’ll need for their first car loan or apartment — years before they understand how credit works.

- Refunds don’t stop the payments. Returns can take weeks to process while the installments keep coming out, so they can still be paying for something that’s already back in the mail.

- Worst of all, it trains instant gratification. It erases the gap between wanting something and owning it — and that pause, the patience to save and wait, is the exact habit that builds real wealth.

Teach them early: “pay later” is a loan dressed up as a discount. The rule that protects them — if you can’t pay for it in full today, you can’t afford it yet.

There’s up to $90,000 in government money most eligible families never claim 👇

It’s called the RDSP, and it’s for Canadians approved for the Disability Tax Credit. The government matches your contributions, as much as 300% depending on your family income. And the bond adds up to $1,000 a year with no contribution required at all, just an open account.

The catch is that it starts with the Disability Tax Credit, which covers far more than most people assume, because it’s about how a condition affects daily life, not the diagnosis. Fewer than one in three eligible families have opened one, usually because they didn’t know it existed.

If someone in your family might qualify, this is worth looking into.

caption:
10 signs you’re ahead of most parents in teaching your kids about money 👇

Think you’re behind on raising money-smart kids? You’re probably doing better than you realize. Here’s what being ahead on financial literacy actually looks like in a Canadian family:

1. You max out the CESG grant available for your kids RESP (only ~1 in 3 Canadian parents do)

2. You talk to your kids about investing (only 4 in 10 parents do)

3. 1 in 4 RESP parents contribute $200/year or less — if you’re putting in steadily, you’re ahead of most.

4. Your kids know money comes from work — not just the “tap” of a card.

5. They have a real place to put money — a jar or an account they actually check.

6. They’ve felt a true trade-off: choosing one thing meant giving up another.

7. They’ve waited and saved for something instead of getting it instantly.

8. They’ve earned money for real work, not just been handed it.

9. They know a “want” from a “need”.

10. They’ve watched you save, give, and spend on purpose.

If even a few of these sound like you, you’re ahead of most. 

Save this as a reminder you’re doing better than you think, and share it with a parent who needs to hear it too.

🏃 Health is wealth — the one asset they can’t buy back later, and every dollar they earn depends on it.

📈 Start investing early — time does more work than money ever will; a decade of compounding beats a bigger paycheque.

💰 Pay yourself first — save before you spend, not whatever’s left over (there’s never anything left over).

🙂 Don’t compare to others — most of what looks like wealth is debt, and comparison is how good savers start overspending.

🧠 Use debt carefully as a tool — debt that buys an asset can build wealth; debt that buys a want quietly destroys it.

caption:
Unpopular opinion: your expenses have a floor, but your earning potential has no ceiling. 👇

Most of us were raised on the first half of that idea, and it’s decent advice as far as it goes. Clip the coupons, turn the lights off, don’t waste. But there’s a limit to how little you can spend, and you can’t cut your way past zero, so eventually that strategy runs out of room.

What about the other half - which is that there’s no equivalent limit on what you can earn. You can learn a skill, build something, ask for more, start a thing on the side, and none of that has a ceiling on it.

If our kids only ever learn to shrink, they’ll spend their whole lives playing defence against a number that can only go so low. So teach them both, because one of those is a limit and the other is a lever.

caption:
The most tax-efficient way to invest for your Canadian child from birth — and most parents have never heard the full strategy. 🍁

Step one is always the RESP. The CESG grant is a guaranteed 20% return on contributions and nothing else comes close. Claim every dollar of it.

But the RESP has a $50,000 lifetime limit, is restricted to education, and expires. It was never designed to build generational wealth.

That’s where the in-trust account comes in. No contribution limits. No restrictions on use. Starts at birth. Invest in XEQT — capital gains compound and are taxed in the child’s hands at their typically near-zero rate.

If done correctly (see comment below), at 18 the child takes control with no/little tax event on the transfer. They sell gradually — ideally when income is low — and move proceeds into their TFSA and FHSA within annual contribution room. The capital gains tax hit at that point is typically negligible. Everything then grows tax-free forever.

RESP funds education. In-trust builds wealth. TFSA and FHSA shelter it permanently.

Three accounts. Each doing a job the others can’t. That’s the complete Canadian strategy. 🍁

The doubling penny is the best way to explain compound interest to a kid.

Ask the question before you show the answer. Let them guess. Almost every child picks the million dollars — and that wrong answer is the whole point.

The number barely moves for the first two weeks. Then it explodes. That is exactly how compound interest works in real life — slow and invisible at first, then faster than anyone expects.

When they see Day 30 the concept clicks in a way no textbook explanation ever will.

78% of Canadians say they’re financially literate. Nearly 6 in 10 failed when actually tested. Millennials were the most confident — and the most likely to fail, with only 31% passing. These are the 5 questions most people got wrong. How many can you get right? 

These 5 questions come from Canada’s national financial literacy survey (CFCS) by Statistics Canada.

Q1: Less. Inflation growing faster than your savings rate means your money loses purchasing power even as your balance grows.

Q2: True. Shorter mortgage = higher payments but far less total interest paid. Often $80,000+ less on a Canadian mortgage.

Q3: Nobody. Bank deposits have CDIC protection. Your investments don’t. This is why staying invested long term matters.

Q4: When it gets you a better paying job. Borrowing to increase earning capacity makes sense. Borrowing for a sale never does.

Q5: Yes. Interest in a regular savings account is taxable. Inside a TFSA — it isn’t. Ever. This is why the TFSA exists.

Studies show an increase in later wages, yes. But when you look more closely at race and socioeconomic status, evidence shows that opportunities and later wealth are not  enjoyed equally. Additionally, there is scant research, but what does exist resulted in a WHO warning against the negative mental and physical effects of certain kinds of adolescent employment.  Overall well-being outside of just a teen’s later purchasing power should be of greater priority when we are try to secure the best futures for our children.

caption:
The #1 mistake Canadian parents make with kids (especially young ones)?

Replacing the broken toy.

It feels like the kind thing to do in the moment. And it is kind. 

But the hidden lesson lands anyway:
“If something breaks or runs out — someone will just get me another one.”

That belief follows kids into adulthood. It shows up in how they handle debt, spending, and the first time life doesn’t replace what they lost.

The alternative isn’t being harsh. Acknowledging that it’s sad. That things break. That money spent is gone. Small losses handled honestly now build the resilience that handles real financial disappointment later.

caption:
1. “Let them feel the disappointment.”
When my daughter ran out of her spending money and couldn’t buy something she wanted — I didn’t top it up. That moment taught her more about budgeting than any conversation I could have had.

2. “Let them pay.”
From age 6 I let my kids hand over the money at stores.
Something about physically giving it away made the value of it click in a way that nothing else did.

3. “Show them the grocery bill.”
I gave my 11-year-old $50 and the weekly grocery list.
She came home $4 under budget and deeply personally offended by the price of cheese. She budgets everything now.

4. “Never say we can’t afford it.”
We replaced it with:
“That’s not where we’re choosing to spend right now.”
My kids grew up understanding that money is managed — not suffered.

5. “Talk about it at dinner.”
Not in a stressful way. Just normally. The way you’d talk about anything that matters.
We talk about what we’re saving toward. What we decided not to buy. What a good decision looks like.

6. “Celebrate the wins.”
When my daughter hit her first savings goal we celebrated like it was a birthday. She’s been chasing that feeling ever since.
We celebrate what we value. Make sure money progress is on that list.

The habits that build wealth aren’t complicated — they’re just not taught early enough. These nine habits, started in childhood, compound the same way money does. 🍁

The earlier your kids learn them the less they have to unlearn as adults.
